setting.tex:
A \emph{language} is any set of strings over $\Sigma$, i.e., any subset of $\Sigma^*$. Let $L$ be a nonempty language. A \emph{positive presentation of} $L$ is an infinite sequence $\sigma = s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots$, of strings such that the set $\{s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots\}$ is precisely $L$. An \emph{indexed family of nonempty languages} is an infinite sequence $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, where each $L_i$ is a nonempty language. An \emph{indexed family of nonempty recursive languages} is an indexed family of nonempty languages $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, such that there exists an effective procedure to compute the membership function
$$\begin{array}{rll} f(i, w) & = 1 & \text{if } w \in L_i \\ & = 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{array}$$

The sequence $M[\sigma]$ is said to \emph{converge to} the positive integer $i$ if and only if either $M[\sigma]$ is infinite and all but finitely many terms of it are equal to $i$, or $M[\sigma]$ is nonnull and finite, and the last term is equal to $i$.

Let $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, be an indexed family of nonempty languages. An inference machine $M$ is said to \emph{infer the language $L_i$ from positive data} if and only if for every positive presentation $\sigma$ of $L_i$, there exists a positive integer $j$ such that $M[\sigma]$ converges to $j$ and $L_j = L_i$. $M$ is said to \emph{infer the family} $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, \emph{from positive data} if and only if for every $i \geqslant 1$ $M$ infers the language $L_i$ from positive data. An indexed family of nonempty languages $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is \emph{inferrable from positive data} if and only if there exists an inference machine $M$ that infers $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, from positive data.

terms.tex:
We say $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, \emph{satisfies Condition 2} provided that, for every $i \geqslant 1$, there exists a finite set $T_i \subseteq L_i$ such that for every $j \geqslant 1$, if $T_i \subseteq L_j$ then $L_j$ is not a proper subset of $L_i$.

Note that Condition 2 is simply Condition 1 with the requirement of effective enumerability of $T_i$ dropped. Also note that the satisfaction of Condition 2 does not depend at all on the indexing of the family of languages, but simply on the set of languages that appear in the sequence.

quotes.tex: An indexed family of nonempty recursive languages is inferrable from positive data if and only if it satisfies Condition 1.

terms.tex:
An indexed family of nonempty languages \emph{satisfies Condition} 1 if and only if there exists an effective procedure which on any input $i \geqslant 1$ enumerates a set of strings $T_i$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $T_i$ is finite,
\item $T_i \subseteq L_i$, and
\item for all $j \geqslant 1$, if $T_i \subseteq L_j$ then $L_j$ is not a proper subset of $L_i$.
\end{enumerate}

The sequence $M[\sigma]$ is said to \emph{converge to} the positive integer $i$ if and only if either $M[\sigma]$ is infinite and all but finitely many terms of it are equal to $i$, or $M[\sigma]$ is nonnull and finite, and the last term is equal to $i$.

Let $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, be an indexed family of nonempty languages. An inference machine $M$ is said to \emph{infer the language $L_i$ from positive data} if and only if for every positive presentation $\sigma$ of $L_i$, there exists a positive integer $j$ such that $M[\sigma]$ converges to $j$ and $L_j = L_i$. $M$ is said to \emph{infer the family} $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, \emph{from positive data} if and only if for every $i \geqslant 1$ $M$ infers the language $L_i$ from positive data. An indexed family of nonempty languages $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is \emph{inferrable from positive data} if and only if there exists an inference machine $M$ that infers $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, from positive data.

quotes.tex: There exists an indexed family of nonempty recursive languages satisfying Condition 2 that is not inferrable from positive data.

terms.tex: We say $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, \emph{satisfies Condition 2} provided that, for every $i \geqslant 1$, there exists a finite set $T_i \subseteq L_i$ such that for every $j \geqslant 1$, if $T_i \subseteq L_j$ then $L_j$ is not a proper subset of $L_i$.

quotes.tex: There exists an indexed family of nonempty recursive languages that is inferrable from positive data but does not satisfy Condition 1$'$.

terms.tex: An indexed family of nonempty recursive sets $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is said to \emph{satisfy Condition 1$'$} provided there exists an effective procedure which on input $i$ outputs the elements of a finite set $T_i$ and then halts, where $T_i \subseteq L_i$ and for all $j \geqslant 1$, if $T_i \subseteq L_j$ then $L_j$ is not a proper subset of $L_i$.

quotes.tex: There exists an indexed family of nonempty recursive languages $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, that is inferrable from positive data but is such that no inference machine $M$ that infers $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, from positive data can be conservative on $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$.

terms.tex: We say $M$ is \emph{conservative on} $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, provided that for every $i \geqslant 1$ and every positive presentation $\sigma$ of $L_i$, if $M$ on input $\sigma$ makes the guess $i$ at some step and then makes the guess $j \neq i$ at some subsequent step, then $L_i$ must fail to contain some input string read prior to the later step.

quotes.tex: Let $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, be an indexed family of nonempty recursive languages that satisfies Conditions 3 and 5. Then there exists an inference machine $M$ that infers $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, from positive data and is consistent, responsive, and conservative on $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$.

terms.tex: Let $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, be an indexed family of nonempty languages. Let $M$ be an inference machine. We say $M$ is \emph{consistent on} $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, provided that for every $i \geqslant 1$ and every positive presentation $\sigma$ of $L_i$, whenever $M$ on input $\sigma$ enters the guess state, the language guessed contains all the input strings read in up to that point in the computation. We say $M$ is \emph{responsive on} $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, provided that for every $i \geqslant 1$ and every positive presentation $\sigma$ of $L_i$, between any two distinct steps of the computation of $M$ on input $\sigma$ in which $M$ is in the request state, there exists a step in which $M$ is in the guess state. We say $M$ is \emph{conservative on} $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, provided that for every $i \geqslant 1$ and every positive presentation $\sigma$ of $L_i$, if $M$ on input $\sigma$ makes the guess $i$ at some step and then makes the guess $j \neq i$ at some subsequent step, then $L_i$ must fail to contain some input string read prior to the later step.

We say $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, \emph{satisfies Condition 3} if for each nonempty finite set $S \subseteq \Sigma^*$, the set $C(S) = \{L \colon S \subseteq L \textit{ and } L = L_i \textit{ for some } i\}$ is of finite cardinality.

Let $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, be an indexed family of nonempty languages. If $S \subseteq \Sigma^*$ and $i \geqslant 1$ then we say $i$ is \emph{descriptive of} $S$ provided $S \subseteq L_i$ and for all $j \geqslant 1$ such that $S \subseteq L_j$, $L_j$ is not a proper subset of $L_i$.

\textsc{Condition} 5. An indexed family of nonempty recursive languages $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is said to satisfy Condition 5 provided there exists a partial recursive function $f$ such that $f(S)$ is some $i$ that is descriptive of $S$ whenever $S$ is a nonempty finite set of strings such that there exists some $j$ that is descriptive of $S$.

quotes.tex: If $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is an indexed family of recursive languages that is inferrable from positive data, then it satisfies Condition 2.

quotes.tex: If $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is an indexed family of nonempty recursive languages such that Condition 3 is satisfied, then it is inferrable from positive data.

quotes.tex: Let $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, be an indexed family of nonempty recursive languages that satisfies Conditions 2 and 4. Then $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, is inferrable from positive data.

terms.tex: We say $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$, \emph{satisfies Condition 2} provided that, for every $i \geqslant 1$, there exists a finite set $T_i \subseteq L_i$ such that for every $j \geqslant 1$, if $T_i \subseteq L_j$ then $L_j$ is not a proper subset of $L_i$.

An indexed family of nonempty recursive languages $L_1, L_2, L_3, \ldots$ is said to \emph{satisfy Condition 4} provided there exists an effective procedure to compute the inclusion function:
$$\begin{array}{rll} h(i, j) & = 1 & \textit{if } L_i \subseteq L_j \\ & = 0 & \textit{otherwise.} \end{array}$$
